DECISION
APPLICATION TO REOPEN
INTRODUCTION

[1] This decision concerns an application, under rule 62 of the Refugee Protection Division Rules (RPD Rules), to reopen the hearing concerning XXXX XXXX (hereinafter the applicant), following a decision rendered by the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) on May 15, 2018, declaring his refugee protection claim had been abandoned.
SUMMARY OF THE FACTS

[2] To briefly summarize the facts in this case, this refugee protection claim was referred to the RPD on March 20, 2018. In accordance with the Practice Notice: Revised Temporary Procedures for providing the Basis of Claim Form in Quebec, the applicant submitted a partial BOC Form on April 13, 2018. It should be noted that the applicant's address in the partial Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form) is in XXXX, British Columbia.

[3] On April 17, 2018, the panel sent a letter to the applicant notifying him that he had to submit his completed BOC Form no later than May 8, 2018, and that if he failed to submit the requested document, he would be required to appear at a special hearing on May 15, 2018, at 9:00 a.m., to provide reasons for this non-compliance. This letter was mailed to the applicant at the address on the record, that is, the address in British Columbia. The letter was also mailed to his counsel of record.

[4] The applicant failed to submit his BOC Form within the allotted time frame and did not attend his special hearing on May 15, 2018, at 9:00 a.m. The panel therefore declared his refugee protection claim to be abandoned that day.

[5] The panel notes that the completed BOC Form was filed on May 15, 2018, that is, the same day as the special hearing and the abandonment decision. The panel also notes that in his BOC Form, the applicant's address is in Montréal.

[6] On October 26, 2018, the applicant's counsel filed an application to reopen this case, stating, in particular, that
* the applicant had had financial difficulties in British Columbia and had moved to Toronto;
* on May 15, 2018, the applicant had returned to Montréal and was present for his special hearing;
* on May 15, 2018, the applicant was in the waiting room and standing by to be called for his special hearing;
* on May 15, 2018, counsel was in room 21 to proceed with VB7-01743;
* the applicant received a letter from the Canada Border Services Agency summoning him for October 27, 2018, for a potential departure from Canada; and
* the applicant never wanted to abandon his refugee protection claim.

[7] On October 29, 2018, the Minister's counsel objected to this application to reopen, stating that the applicant had failed to establish a breach of natural justice. In his response, the Minister's counsel mentioned that the applicant's removal was scheduled for November 3, 2018.
ANALYSIS

[8] The RPD has very limited jurisdiction with respect to reopening a hearing. Once it has rendered a decision, the RPD has discharged its duty (functus officio) and cannot exercise it a second time in the same case, except when there has been a violation of the rules of natural justice.1

[9] To reach a decision in this application to reopen, the panel considered the entire record, as well as subrule 62(6) of the RPD Rules.

[10] The applicant's counsel stated that he was present on May 15, 2018, and was proceeding in file VB7-01743.

[11] The panel looked into this matter and notes that it is true that the applicant's counsel proceeded with another case on May 15, 2018. However, it should be noted that the case in question was a Vancouver case, in which the hearing was scheduled for 7:45 a.m., Pacific Standard Time (PST). Considering the time difference between the regions, this means that the hearing was to start at 10:45 a.m., Montréal time. It is important to note that, according to our records management system, counsel in VB7-01743 arrived late, at 9:15 a.m. (PST), which is 12:15 p.m. in Montréal.

[12] Given that the applicant's special hearing was scheduled for 9:00 a.m. (Montréal time), the panel can only conclude that counsel of record was definitely available to represent his client at the special hearing because he was not in a hearing room at that time for another case. However, he did not come. The application to reopen does not address this point, and the panel wonders why.

[13] The applicant alleges that he was present on May 15, 2018, waiting to be called for his special hearing. The panel is surprised by this statement and, if it is true, it wonders why the applicant did not go to the reception area to let them know that he was there, as all applicants do when they attend a hearing. The application to reopen does not provide any explanation on this point, and the panel wonders why.

[14] The application to reopen provides few details with respect to how long the applicant waited to be called or when he left. In addition, the panel has difficulty understanding why his counsel would not have appeared in the hearing room at 9:00 a.m. or, at the very least, would not have notified the reception desk that the applicant was there. The panel notes again that the application to reopen does not address this important point. Once more, the panel wonders why.

[15] The panel also struggles to understand why the applicant and his counsel did not act more diligently if, as they claim, the applicant waited in vain to be called for his special hearing. The application to reopen was filed more than five months after the refugee protection claim was declared abandoned, even though the notice of decision regarding the abandonment of the claim was sent to them on May 25, 2018. The panel also notes that the application to reopen was filed after a summons for his removal was received. The application to reopen does not provide any explanation on this subject.

[16] It must be noted that the explanations provided in the application to reopen lack detail, and the panel finds that this undermines the applicant's credibility.

[17] In addition, the panel notes an important fact.

[18] The Division sent a letter to the applicant and his counsel on April 17, 2018, requesting that they submit the completed BOC Form no later than May 8, 2018. The panel notes that the completed BOC Form was submitted on May 15, 2018, that is, the same day as the abandonment hearing. Curiously, the panel notes that the applicant's signature in the completed BOC Form is not an original signature, but rather a photocopy, and is also dated March 12, 2018. However, on that date, he had not yet been asked for his completed BOC Form. In fact, page 11 of the completed BOC Form, which contains the applicant's signature and the date of his signature, is a photocopy of page 11 of the partial BOC Form submitted on April 10, 2018.

APPLICATION TO REOPEN
INTRODUCTION

[1] This decision concerns an application, under rule 62 of the Refugee Protection Division Rules (RPD Rules), to reopen the hearing concerning XXXX XXXX (hereinafter the applicant), following a decision rendered by the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) on May 15, 2018, declaring his refugee protection claim had been abandoned.
SUMMARY OF THE FACTS

[2] To briefly summarize the facts in this case, this refugee protection claim was referred to the RPD on March 20, 2018. In accordance with the Practice Notice: Revised Temporary Procedures for providing the Basis of Claim Form in Quebec, the applicant submitted a partial BOC Form on April 13, 2018. This letter was mailed to the applicant at the address on the record, that is, the address in British Columbia. The letter was also mailed to his counsel of record.

[4] The applicant failed to submit his BOC Form within the allotted time frame and did not attend his special hearing on May 15, 2018, at 9:00 a.m. The panel therefore declared his refugee protection claim to be abandoned that day.

[5] The panel notes that the completed BOC Form was filed on May 15, 2018, that is, the same day as the special hearing and the abandonment decision. The panel also notes that in his BOC Form, the applicant's address is in Montréal.

[6] On October 26, 2018, the applicant's counsel filed an application to reopen this case, stating, in particular, that
* the applicant had had financial difficulties in British Columbia and had moved to Toronto;
* on May 15, 2018, the applicant had returned to Montréal and was present for his special hearing;
* on May 15, 2018, the applicant was in the waiting room and standing by to be called for his special hearing;
* on May 15, 2018, counsel was in room 21 to proceed with VB7-01743;
* the applicant received a letter from the Canada Border Services Agency summoning him for October 27, 2018, for a potential departure from Canada; and
* the applicant never wanted to abandon his refugee protection claim.

[7] On October 29, 2018, the Minister's counsel objected to this application to reopen, stating that the applicant had failed to establish a breach of natural justice. In his response, the Minister's counsel mentioned that the applicant's removal was scheduled for November 3, 2018.
ANALYSIS

[8] The RPD has very limited jurisdiction with respect to reopening a hearing. Once it has rendered a decision, the RPD has discharged its duty (functus officio) and cannot exercise it a second time in the same case, except when there has been a violation of the rules of natural justice.1

[9] To reach a decision in this application to reopen, the panel considered the entire record, as well as subrule 62(6) of the RPD Rules.

[10] The applicant's counsel stated that he was present on May 15, 2018, and was proceeding in file VB7-01743.

[11] The panel looked into this matter and notes that it is true that the applicant's counsel proceeded with another case on May 15, 2018. However, it should be noted that the case in question was a Vancouver case, in which the hearing was scheduled for 7:45 a.m., Pacific Standard Time (PST). Considering the time difference between the regions, this means that the hearing was to start at 10:45 a.m., Montréal time. It is important to note that, according to our records management system, counsel in VB7-01743 arrived late, at 9:15 a.m. (PST), which is 12:15 p.m. in Montréal.

[12] Given that the applicant's special hearing was scheduled for 9:00 a.m. (Montréal time), the panel can only conclude that counsel of record was definitely available to represent his client at the special hearing because he was not in a hearing room at that time for another case. However, he did not come. The application to reopen does not address this point, and the panel wonders why.

[13] The applicant alleges that he was present on May 15, 2018, waiting to be called for his special hearing. The panel is surprised by this statement and, if it is true, it wonders why the applicant did not go to the reception area to let them know that he was there, as all applicants do when they attend a hearing. The application to reopen does not provide any explanation on this point, and the panel wonders why.

[14] The application to reopen provides few details with respect to how long the applicant waited to be called or when he left. In addition, the panel has difficulty understanding why his counsel would not have appeared in the hearing room at 9:00 a.m. or, at the very least, would not have notified the reception desk that the applicant was there. The panel notes again that the application to reopen does not address this important point. Once more, the panel wonders why.

[15] The panel also struggles to understand why the applicant and his counsel did not act more diligently if, as they claim, the applicant waited in vain to be called for his special hearing. The application to reopen was filed more than five months after the refugee protection claim was declared abandoned, even though the notice of decision regarding the abandonment of the claim was sent to them on May 25, 2018. The panel also notes that the application to reopen was filed after a summons for his removal was received. The application to reopen does not provide any explanation on this subject.

[16] It must be noted that the explanations provided in the application to reopen lack detail, and the panel finds that this undermines the applicant's credibility.

[17] In addition, the panel notes an important fact.

[18] The Division sent a letter to the applicant and his counsel on April 17, 2018, requesting that they submit the completed BOC Form no later than May 8, 2018. The panel notes that the completed BOC Form was submitted on May 15, 2018, that is, the same day as the abandonment hearing. Curiously, the panel notes that the applicant's signature in the completed BOC Form is not an original signature, but rather a photocopy, and is also dated March 12, 2018. However, on that date, he had not yet been asked for his completed BOC Form. In fact, page 11 of the completed BOC Form, which contains the applicant's signature and the date of his signature, is a photocopy of page 11 of the partial BOC Form submitted on April 10, 2018.

[19] If the applicant was in Montréal on May 15, 2018, as he claims in his application to reopen, the panel does not understand why he would not have signed the document himself and written the correct date on it. The application to reopen does not address this issue, and the panel finds that this seriously undermines the applicant's credibility.

subthemes.text:
[20] Counsel alleges that the applicant does not have a fixed address in Montréal. His affidavit in support of his application to reopen was signed in Toronto on October 25, 2018. Curiously, although this affidavit was signed in Toronto, the applicant states in it that he lives in Vancouver. The panel is therefore confused about where the applicant lives and where he actually is. This issue is also unclear in the allegations in the application to reopen.

[21] In light of the above, the panel does not find the applicant's explanations for not attending the special hearing on May 15, 2018, credible. The panel simply does not believe that he was in Montréal on that date. Moreover, no documents were filed to support this statement (an airplane ticket, train ticket, bus ticket, etc.). He bears the burden of proof, and if he wanted to establish that he was in Montréal and present for the hearing on May 15, 2018, it was his responsibility to file evidence to that effect. However, he did not do so. His credibility is irreparably undermined.

[22] In light of the foregoing, the panel concludes that the applicant has failed to discharge his burden of establishing a breach of natural justice.

[23] After reviewing this application, the panel concludes that there was no breach of the principles of natural justice as, throughout the process, the RPD followed the legal procedure and applied the rules of natural justice.
CONCLUSION

[18] The Division sent a letter to the applicant and his counsel on April 17, 2018, requesting that they submit the completed BOC Form no later than May 8, 2018. The panel notes that the completed BOC Form was submitted on May 15, 2018, that is, the same day as the abandonment hearing. Curiously, the panel notes that the applicant's signature in the completed BOC Form is not an original signature, but rather a photocopy, and is also dated March 12, 2018. However, on that date, he had not yet been asked for his completed BOC Form. In fact, page 11 of the completed BOC Form, which contains the applicant's signature and the date of his signature, is a photocopy of page 11 of the partial BOC Form submitted on April 10, 2018.

[19] If the applicant was in Montréal on May 15, 2018, as he claims in his application to reopen, the panel does not understand why he would not have signed the document himself and written the correct date on it. The application to reopen does not address this issue, and the panel finds that this seriously undermines the applicant's credibility.

[20] Counsel alleges that the applicant does not have a fixed address in Montréal. His affidavit in support of his application to reopen was signed in Toronto on October 25, 2018. Curiously, although this affidavit was signed in Toronto, the applicant states in it that he lives in Vancouver. The panel is therefore confused about where the applicant lives and where he actually is. This issue is also unclear in the allegations in the application to reopen.

[21] In light of the above, the panel does not find the applicant's explanations for not attending the special hearing on May 15, 2018, credible. The panel simply does not believe that he was in Montréal on that date. Moreover, no documents were filed to support this statement (an airplane ticket, train ticket, bus ticket, etc.). He bears the burden of proof, and if he wanted to establish that he was in Montréal and present for the hearing on May 15, 2018, it was his responsibility to file evidence to that effect. However, he did not do so. His credibility is irreparably undermined.
[22] In light of the foregoing, the panel concludes that the applicant has failed to discharge his burden of establishing a breach of natural justice.

[23] After reviewing this application, the panel concludes that there was no breach of the principles of natural justice as, throughout the process, the RPD followed the legal procedure and applied the rules of natural justice.
CONCLUSION

[24] For these reasons, the application to reopen is dismissed.
